canonical_examples.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,\neg A \land \neg B \,$ | $\,\neg (A \lor B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |

Use your results to determine whether $\neg A \land \neg B$ is logically equivalent to $\neg (A \lor B).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A \equiv \textrm T$ and $B \equiv \textrm F,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬A∧¬B & ≡¬\text{T}∧¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A \equiv \textrm F$ and $B \equiv \textrm T,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∨B) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A \equiv \textrm F$ and $B \equiv \textrm F,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∨B) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,\neg A \land \neg B \,$ | $\,\neg (A \lor B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

 

To determine whether $\neg A \land \neg B$ is logically equivalent to $\neg (A \lor B),$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same $(\textrm{F},\textrm{F},\textrm{F},\textrm{T}).$ Therefore, we conclude that $\neg A \land \neg B$ is logically equivalent to $\neg (A \lor B),$ that is,

$$
\neg A \land \neg B \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\equiv} \neg (A \lor B).
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Two statements are **logically equivalent** if they have identical truth values in their respective truth tables. In this lesson, we'll use truth tables to show that two complex compound statements are logically equivalent. 

If two statements $P$ and $Q$ are logically equivalent, we write

$$
P\equiv Q
$$

where the symbol "$\equiv$" means "is logically equivalent to."

For example, let's use a truth table to prove the following logical equivalence:

$$
(A \land \neg A) \lor B \equiv B
$$

First, we construct truth tables with columns $A$ and $B$ containing all possible combinations of truth values. Then, we create another column for $\neg A,$ which has the opposite truth values to $A.$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, \neg A \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing a Truth Table
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A \equiv \textrm T$ and $B \equiv \textrm F,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬A∧¬B & ≡¬\text{T}∧¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A \equiv \textrm F$ and $B \equiv \textrm T,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∨B) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A \equiv \textrm F$ and $B \equiv \textrm F,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∨B) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,\neg A \land \neg B \,$ | $\,\neg (A \lor B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

 

To determine whether $\neg A \land \neg B$ is logically equivalent to $\neg (A \lor B),$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same $(\textrm{F},\textrm{F},\textrm{F},\textrm{T}).$ Therefore, we conclude that $\neg A \land \neg B$ is logically equivalent to $\neg (A \lor B),$ that is,

$$
\neg A \land \neg B \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\equiv} \neg (A \lor B).
$$

  • When P≡T and Q≡F, we have (P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q)≡(T∨F)∧¬(T∧¬F)≡T∧¬T≡T∧F≡F

  • When P≡F and Q≡T, we have (P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q)≡(F∨T)∧¬(F∧¬T)≡T∧¬F≡T∧T≡T

To determine whether (P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q) is logically equivalent to Q, we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same (T,F,T,F). Therefore, we conclude that

(P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q)≡Q.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying Equivalent Statements Using Partially Completed Truth Tables
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬P∨Q & ≡¬\text{T}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{F}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨Q)\,$ | $\,¬P∨Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

To determine whether $¬(P∨Q)$ is logically equivalent to $¬P∨Q,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are *different* (one is $\text{F},\text{F},\text{F},\text{T}$, while the other is $\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T}$). Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
¬(P∨Q)\text{⧸}≢¬P∨Q.
$$

First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B) & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{T})∨¬(\text{T}∨¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{T})∨¬(\text{T}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∨¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B) & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{F})∨¬(\text{T}∨¬\text{F}) \\  & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{F})∨¬(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∨¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{F}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B) & ≡(\text{F}∧\text{T})∨¬(\text{F}∨¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∨¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

To determine whether $(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)$ is logically equivalent to $A,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

We see that the columns for $(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)$ and $A$ are different. They differ in the second and third rows. Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)≢A.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Completing a Truth Table

solution.reasoning: If A is true, A∨B is true, so ¬(A∨B) is false. If A is false, the conjunction A∧¬(A∨B) is already false. Thus the conjunction is false in every row, and its negation is true in all four rows. question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∨B)∧A\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
question.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for the part of the expression that's in parentheses, $A∨B:$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∨B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for the negation, $¬(A∨B):$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∨B\,$ | $\,¬(A∨B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Finally, we add a column for $¬(A∨B)∧A:$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∨B\,$ | $\,¬(A∨B)\,$ | $\,¬(A∨B)∧A\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Find the missing values in the following truth table:
A B ¬(A∨B)∧A
T T
T
F
T
T F
F
F
T
F T
F
F
T

F

EXPLANATION

First, we add a column for the part of the expression that's in parentheses, A∨B:

A B A∨B
T T T
T F T
F T T
F F F

Then, we add a column for the negation, ¬(A∨B):

A B A∨B ¬(A∨B)
T T T F
T F T F
F T T F
F F F T

Finally, we add a column for ¬(A∨B)∧A:

A B A∨B ¬(A∨B) ¬(A∨B)∧A
T T T F F
T F T F F
F T T F F
F F F T F
question.knowledge_point: Completing a Truth Table

solution.reasoning: When A is true, A∨B is true, so ¬(A∨B) is false and the conjunction is false. When A is false, the conjunction with A is false regardless of B. Therefore all four entries are F. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different expression.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧¬(A∧B))\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
question.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for the part of the expression that's in parentheses, $A∧B:$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

 

Then, we add a column for $¬(A∧B):$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Next, we add the column for $A∧¬(A∧B):$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ | $\,A∧¬(A∧B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Finally, we add the column for $¬(A∧¬(A∧B))):$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ | $\,A∧¬(A∧B)\,$ | $\,¬(A∧¬(A∧B))\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

EXPLANATION

First, we add a column for the part of the expression that's in parentheses, A∧B:

A B A∧B
T T T
T F F
F T F
F F F

Then, we add a column for ¬(A∧B):

A B A∧B ¬(A∧B)
T T T F
T F F T
F T F T
F F F T

Next, we add the column for A∧¬(A∧B):

A B A∧B ¬(A∧B) A∧¬(A∧B)
T T T F F
T F F T T
F T F T F
F F F T F

Finally, we add the column for ¬(A∧¬(A∧B))):

A B A∧B ¬(A∧B) A∧¬(A∧B) ¬(A∧¬(A∧B))
T T T F F T

question.knowledge_point: Completing a Truth Table

solution.reasoning: When A is true, A∧B equals B, so ¬(A∧¬(A∧B)) equals ¬¬B=B. This gives T and F in the first two rows. When A is false, the conjunction inside the outer negation is false, giving T in both remaining rows. question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,B∨(¬A∧¬B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
question.worked_solution:
First, let's add columns for $¬A$ and $¬B:$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,¬B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Then, we add a column for the part of the expression that's in parentheses, $¬A∧¬B:$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,¬B\,$ | $\,¬A∧¬B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Finally, we add a column for $B∨(¬A∧¬B):$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,¬B\,$ | $\,¬A∧¬B\,$ | $\,B∨(¬A∧¬B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

question.knowledge_point: Completing a Truth Table

solution.reasoning: When B is true, the disjunction is true, giving T in rows 1 and 3. When B is false, ¬B is true and the expression equals ¬A, giving F in row 2 and T in row 4. Thus the answers are T, F, T, T. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different expression.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,(P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

 

Using your results, complete the following statement:

$$
(P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q){{field-4}}Q
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(P∨Q)∧¬(P\text{ }∧¬Q) & ≡(\text{T}∨\text{T})∧¬(\text{T}∧¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q) & ≡(\text{T}∨\text{F})∧¬(\text{T}∧¬\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}∧\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{F}$ and $Q≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(P∨Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q) & ≡(\text{F}∨\text{T})∧¬(\text{F}∧¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨Q)\,$ | $\,¬P∨Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-3}} | $\text{T}$ |

Using your results, complete the following statement:

$$
¬(P∨Q){{field-4}}¬P∨Q
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬P∨Q & ≡¬\text{T}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{F}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨Q)\,$ | $\,¬P∨Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

To determine whether $¬(P∨Q)$ is logically equivalent to $¬P∨Q,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are *different* (one is $\text{F},\text{F},\text{F},\text{T}$, while the other is $\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T}$). Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
¬(P∨Q)\text{⧸}≢¬P∨Q.
$$

$$

$$

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬P∨Q & ≡¬\text{T}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{F}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨Q)\,$ | $\,¬P∨Q\,$ |

| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are *different* (one is $\text{F},\text{F},\text{F},\text{T}$, while the other is $\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T}$). Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
¬(P∨Q)\text{⧸}≢¬P∨Q.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{T}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬P∨Q & ≡¬\text{T}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $P≡\text{F}$ and $Q≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬(\text{F}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨Q)\,$ | $\,¬P∨Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

To determine whether $¬(P∨Q)$ is logically equivalent to $¬P∨Q,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are *different* (one is $\text{F},\text{F},\text{F},\text{T}$, while the other is $\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T}$). Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
¬(P∨Q)\text{⧸}≢¬P∨Q.
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧(B∨¬A)\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Using your results, complete the following statement:

$$
A∧(B∨¬A){{field-4}}A∧B
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧(B∨¬A) & ≡\text{T}∧(\text{T}∨¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧(\text{T}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧B & ≡\text{T}∧\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{F}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧(B∨¬A) & ≡\text{F}∧(\text{T}∨¬\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∧(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧(B∨¬A)\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

To determine whether $A∧(B∨¬A)$ is logically equivalent to $A∧B,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.  

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{F},\text{F}).$ Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
A∧(B∨¬A)≡A∧B.
$$

A∧(B∨¬A)≡A∧B.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧(B∨¬A) & ≡\text{T}∧(\text{T}∨¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧(\text{T}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧B & ≡\text{T}∧\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{F}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧(B∨¬A) & ≡\text{F}∧(\text{T}∨¬\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∧(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∧\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧(B∨¬A)\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

To determine whether $A∧(B∨¬A)$ is logically equivalent to $A∧B,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.  

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{F},\text{F}).$ Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
A∧(B∨¬A)≡A∧B.
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧¬B)\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Using your results, complete the following statement:

$$
¬(A∧¬B){{field-4}}¬A∨B
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∧¬B) & ≡¬(\text{T}∧¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬(\text{T}∧\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬A∨B & ≡¬\text{T}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{F}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∧¬B) & ≡¬(\text{F}∧¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬(\text{F}∧\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below. 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧¬B)\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

To determine whether $¬(A∧¬B)$ is logically equivalent to $¬A∨B,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T}).$ Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
¬(A∧¬B)≡¬A∨B.
$$

EXPLANATION

  • When A≡T and B≡T, we have ¬(A∧¬B)≡¬(T∧¬T)≡¬(T∧F)≡¬F≡T

  • When A≡T and B≡F, we have ¬A∨B≡¬T∨F≡F∨F≡F

  • When A≡F and B≡T, we have ¬(A∧¬B)≡¬(F∧¬T)≡¬(F∧F)≡¬F≡T

feedback.worked_solution:

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∧¬B) & ≡¬(\text{T}∧¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬(\text{T}∧\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬A∨B & ≡¬\text{T}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{F}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(A∧¬B) & ≡¬(\text{F}∧¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡¬(\text{F}∧\text{F}) \\  & ≡¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below. 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧¬B)\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

To determine whether $¬(A∧¬B)$ is logically equivalent to $¬A∨B,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

Looking at the last two columns, we see that they are the same $(\text{T},\text{F},\text{T},\text{T}).$ Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
¬(A∧¬B)≡¬A∨B.

question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

 

Using your results, complete the following statement:

$$
(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B){{field-4}}A
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's solve for the missing values:

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B) & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{T})∨¬(\text{T}∨¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{T})∨¬(\text{T}∨\text{F}) \\  & ≡\text{T}∨¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{T}$ and $B≡\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B) & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{F})∨¬(\text{T}∨¬\text{F}) \\  & ≡(\text{T}∧\text{F})∨¬(\text{T}∨\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∨¬\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}\end{aligned}
$$

- When $A≡\text{F}$ and $B≡\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B) & ≡(\text{F}∧\text{T})∨¬(\text{F}∨¬\text{T}) \\  & ≡\text{F}∨¬\text{F} \\  & ≡\text{F}∨\text{T} \\  & ≡\text{T}\end{aligned}
$$

Our completed table is shown below.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

To determine whether $(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)$ is logically equivalent to $A,$ we need to check whether their truth tables are equivalent.

We see that the columns for $(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)$ and $A$ are different. They differ in the second and third rows. Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
(A∧B)∨¬(A∨¬B)≢A.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are logically equivalent?

I. $¬X∧(X∨¬Y)$

II. $¬X∨(X∧¬Y)$

III. $¬(X∨(¬X∧Y))$
question.worked_solution:
Two statements are logically equivalent if they have the same truth table. So, we construct a truth table for the three given statements:

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,¬X∧(X∨¬Y)\,$ | $\,¬X∨(X∧¬Y)\,$ | $\,¬(X∨(¬X∧Y))\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

We see that only the statements $¬X∧(X∨¬Y)$ and $¬(X∨(¬X∧Y))$ have the same truth table, so they are logically equivalent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: An eigenvector of $D=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 10 \\ -7 & 11\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda =6$ is  $[\begin{aligned}c \\ 14\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $c.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $D$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Dv=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Dv & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}-8 & 10 \\ -7 & 11\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}c \\ 14\end{aligned}] & =6[\begin{aligned}c \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-8c+140 \\ -7c+154\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6c \\ 84\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8c+140=6c \\ -7c+154=84\end{aligned}
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get

$$
-8c+140=6c\,⟹\,c=10.
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the second equation, we get

$$
-7c+154=84\,⟹\,c=10.
$$

Therefore, the solution of the system is $c=10.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3k+1 & 3\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-k$ is  $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3k+1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =-k[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3k+16\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-k \\ -5k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=-k, \\ 3k+16=-5k\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
2=-k\,⟹\,k=-2.
$$

Now, substituting $k=-2$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3k+16 & =-5k \\ 3\cdot (-2)+16 & =-5\cdot (-2) \\ 10 & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=-2.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $v$ is an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\frac{1}{3}$ then $v$ is also an eigenvector of the matrix ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =4.$

II. An eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is also an eigenvector of the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.$

III. If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$ then $5v$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =15.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement is false. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=\frac{1}{3}v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $3$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=3v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $3.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is true. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(5v)=5Av=5(3v)=3(5v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(5v)=3(5v),$ and $5v\ne 0,$ this implies that $5v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =3.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement is false. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=\frac{1}{3}v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $3$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=3v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $3.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is true. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(5v)=5Av=5(3v)=3(5v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(5v)=3(5v),$ and $5v\ne 0,$ this implies that $5v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =3.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3k+1 & 3\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-k$ is  $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3k+1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] & =-k[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3k+16\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-k \\ -5k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=-k, \\ 3k+16=-5k\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
2=-k\,⟹\,k=-2.
$$

Now, substituting $k=-2$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3k+16 & =-5k \\ 3\cdot (-2)+16 & =-5\cdot (-2) \\ 10 & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=-2.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $v$ is an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\frac{1}{3}$ then $v$ is also an eigenvector of the matrix ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =4.$

II. An eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is also an eigenvector of the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.$

III. If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$ then $5v$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =15.$
question.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement is false. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=\frac{1}{3}v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $3$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=3v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $3.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is true. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(5v)=5Av=5(3v)=3(5v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(5v)=3(5v),$ and $5v\ne 0,$ this implies that $5v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =3.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The distance $d$, in meters, a falling body travels after being released from rest varies directly with the **square** of the time $t,$ measured in seconds, since the body was released. If the body covers $12$ meters in $2$ seconds, then what is the constant of variation?
questions.worked_solution:
The distance $d$ is directly proportional to the square of the time $t$, so we have

$$
d=k{t}^{2},
$$

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $d=12\,\text{m}$ when $t=2\,\text{s}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =k\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 12 & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{12}{4} & =k \\ 3 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the constant of variation is $k=3.$

Question 1
?

The distance d, in meters, a falling body travels after being released from rest varies directly with the square of the time t, measured in seconds, since the body was released. If the body covers 12 meters in 2 seconds, then what is the constant of variation?

a
7
b
4
c
6
d
3
e
5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The distance d is directly proportional to the square of the time t, so we have d=kt2,

where k is the constant of variation.

We are told that d=12m when t=2s. We can use this information to solve for k, as follows:

12=k⋅2212=k⋅4124=k3=k

Therefore, the constant of variation is k=3.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: The surface $S,$ in square centimeters, of a cylinder whose height equals the radius of its base varies directly with the **square** of its radius $r,$ measured in centimeters. If the surface is $16\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}$ when the radius is $2\,\text{cm},$ then what is the constant of variation?
question.worked_solution:
The surface $S$ is directly proportional to the radius $r,$ so we have

$$
S=k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $S=16\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}$ when $r=2\,\text{cm}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16\pi  & =k\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 16\pi  & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{16\pi }{4} & =k \\ 4\pi  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the constant of variation is $k=4\pi .$

question.name: Question 3
question.worked_solution:
The electrostatic force $F$ is directly proportional to the square of the charge $q,$ so we have

$$
F=k{q}^{2},
$$

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $F=8\,976\,\text{N}$ when $q=2\,\text{C}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8\,976 & =k\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 8\,976 & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{8\,976}{4} & =k \\ 2\,244 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our direct variation equation is

$$
F=2\,244{q}^{2}.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+2(\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{18} \\ \frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{13}{18}+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A particular town has a fleet of $720$ bicycles for rent. The table below gives the pattern of rental and return locations over a typical day.
From:
Museum Station Gym
To: Museum $0.9$ $0.3$ $0.1$
Station $0$ $0.3$ $0.7$
Gym $0.1$ $0.4$ $0.2$
For example, $40%$ of the bicycles at the Station are moved to the Gym every day. How many bicycles would eventually be located at the Station if the listed probabilities remained constant over many days?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+3({x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many days, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 720=120.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.35 & 0.45 & 0.6 \\ 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{65} \\ \frac{30}{65} \\ \frac{17}{65}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $q$ is a stochastic vector

II. $Pq=q$

III. $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
Pq=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.35 & 0.45 & 0.6 \\ 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{65} \\ \frac{30}{65} \\ \frac{17}{65}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{65}+\frac{9}{65}+0 \\ \frac{6.3}{65}+\frac{13.5}{65}+\frac{10.2}{65} \\ \frac{2.7}{65}+\frac{7.5}{65}+\frac{6.8}{65}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{65} \\ \frac{30}{65} \\ \frac{17}{65}\end{aligned}]=q.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector such that $Pq=q.$ So, it's a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.75{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 75{x}_{1}-60{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9} \\ \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{9}=-\frac{1}{9}.$

questions.problem:
A factory produces two types of sugar: brown and extra-refined. Every year, the factory's sales executives study how customers' preferences change between the two types of sugar. The table below shows the results of this study.
From:
Brown Extra-Refined
To: Brown $0.8$ $1$
Extra-Refined $0.2$ $0$
It's found that $20%$ of customers who currently buy brown sugar will switch to extra-refined sugar next year, while $100%$ of customers who currently purchase extra-refined sugar will switch to brown sugar next year. Assuming that there are $450\,000$ customers in total and that the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many customers will eventually consume extra-refined sugar?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, note that

$$
{P}^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.84 & 0.8 \\ 0.16 & 0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 \\ 0.2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=5{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the customers will eventually use extra-refined sugar. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this type of sugar is

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 450\,000=75\,000.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+2(\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{18} \\ \frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{13}{18}+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.10.20.300.1−0.80.1000.6−0.40]R1:=10R1R2:=10R2R3:=10R3∼[−12301−81006−40]R2:=R2+R1∼[−12300−64006−40]R3:=R3+(−1)R2∼[−12300−6400000]

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the 1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=23x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −x1+2(23x3)+3x3=0⟹x1=133x3. Hence, the general solution is

$$

As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

$$

$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+3({x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many days, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 720=120.
$$

question.problem:
A particular town has a fleet of $720$ bicycles for rent. The table below gives the pattern of rental and return locations over a typical day.
From:
Museum Station Gym
To: Museum $0.9$ $0.3$ $0.1$
Station $0$ $0.3$ $0.7$
Gym $0.1$ $0.4$ $0.2$

[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

So, after many days, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 720=120.
$$

Question 2

A particular town has a fleet of 720 bicycles for rent. The table below gives the pattern of rental and return locations over a typical day.

From:
Museum Station Gym
To: Museum 0.9 0.3 0.1
Station 0 0.3 0.7
Gym 0.1 0.4 0.2

For example, 40% of the bicycles at the Station are moved to the Gym every day.

How many bicycles would eventually be located at the Station if the listed probabilities remained constant over many days?

a
30
b
480
c
120
d
60
e
240
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix

P=[0.90.30.100.30.70.10.40.2].

Notice that the matrix P2 contains only positive entries. So, the matrix P is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of P, and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=q⟹(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.90.30.100.30.70.10.40.2]−[100010001]=[−0.10.30.10−0.70.70.10.4−0.8].

The matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.10.30.100−0.70.700.10.4−0.80]R1:=10R1R2:=10R2R3:=10R3∼[−13100−77014−80]R3:=R3+R1∼[−13100−77007−70]R3:=R3+R2∼[−13100−7700000]

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the 1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −x1+3(x3)+x3=0⟹x1=4x3. Hence, the general solution is

[4x3x3x3],x3∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have

4x3+x3+x3=16x3=1x3=16.

Therefore,

q=[231616].

So, after many days, 16 of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

16⋅720=120.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.75{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 75{x}_{1}-60{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9} \\ \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{9}=-\frac{1}{9}.$

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 \\ 0.2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=5{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the customers will eventually use extra-refined sugar. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this type of sugar is

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 450\,000=75\,000.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

A factory produces two types of sugar: brown and extra-refined. Every year, the factory's sales executives study how customers' preferences change between the two types of sugar. The table below shows the results of this study.

From:
Brown Extra-Refined
To: Brown 0.8 1
Extra-Refined 0.2 0

It's found that 20% of customers who currently buy brown sugar will switch to extra-refined sugar next year, while 100% of customers who currently purchase extra-refined sugar will switch to brown sugar next year.

Assuming that there are 450000 customers in total and that the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many customers will eventually consume extra-refined sugar?

a
80000
b
90000
c
85000
d
75000
e
65000
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix P=[0.810.20].

Now, note that P2=[0.840.80.160.2].

The matrix P2 contains only positive entries. So, the matrix P is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of P, and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=q⟹(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.810.20]−[1001]=[−0.210.2−1].

So, the matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.2100.2−10]R2:=R2+R1∼[−0.210000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=5x2.

Hence, the general solution is [5x2x2],x2∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have 5x2+x2=16x2=1x2=16.

Therefore, q=[5616].

So, 16 of the customers will eventually use extra-refined sugar. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this type of sugar is 16⋅450000=75000.

question.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+2(\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{18} \\ \frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{13}{18}+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & -8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+2(\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{18} \\ \frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{13}{18}+\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Question 1
?

P=[0.90.20.30.10.20.100.60.6],q=[abc]

Given that q is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix P shown above, what is the value of a+b−c?

a
56
b
−518
c
16
d
13
e
23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=qPq−q=0Pq−Iq=0(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.90.20.30.10.20.100.60.6]−[100010001]=[−0.10.20.30.1−0.80.100.6−0.4].

The matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.10.20.300.1−0.80.1000.6−0.40]R1:=10R1R2:=10R2R3:=10R3∼[−12301−81006−40]R2:=R2+R1∼[−12300−64006−40]R3:=R3+(−1)R2∼[−12300−6400000]

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the 1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=23x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −x1+2(23x3)+3x3=0⟹x1=133x3. Hence, the general solution is

[133x323x3x3],x3∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have

133x3+23x3+x3=16x3=1x3=16.

Therefore,

q=[abc]=[13181916].

Finally,

a+b−c=1318+19−16=23.

solution.reasoning: A steady-state probability vector satisfies Pq=q and a+b+c=1. The third row gives c=3b/2, and the first gives a=2b+3c=13b/2. Thus 9b=1, so (a,b,c)=(13/18,1/9,1/6), yielding a+b-c=2/3. The mathematics is resolved, but no Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was supplied.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
A particular town has a fleet of $720$ bicycles for rent. The table below gives the pattern of rental and return locations over a typical day.
From:
Museum Station Gym
To: Museum $0.9$ $0.3$ $0.1$
Station $0$ $0.3$ $0.7$
Gym $0.1$ $0.4$ $0.2$
For example, $40%$ of the bicycles at the Station are moved to the Gym every day. How many bicycles would eventually be located at the Station if the listed probabilities remained constant over many days?
question.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.9 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0 & 0.3 & 0.7 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$

From:
Museum Station Gym
To: Museum 0.9 0.3 0.1
Station 0 0.3 0.7

a
30
b
480
c
120
d
60
e
240

P=[0.90.30.100.30.70.10.40.2].

Notice that the matrix P2 contains only positive entries. So, the matrix P is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of P, and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=q⟹(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.90.30.100.30.70.10.40.2]−[100010001]=[−0.10.30.10−0.70.70.10.4−0.8].

M=[−0.10.30.100−0.70.700.10.4−0.80]R1:=10R1R2:=10R2R3:=10R3∼[−13100−77014−80]R3:=R3+R1∼[−13100−77007−70]R3:=R3+R2∼[−13100−7700000]

[4x3x3x3],x3∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have

4x3+x3+x3=16x3=1x3=16.

Therefore,

q=[231616].

\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.7 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+3({x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many days, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the bicycles will be at the station. Therefore, the total number of bikes at the station after many days will be

$$
\frac{1}{6}\cdot 720=120.
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

II. $Pq=q$

III. $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
Pq=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.35 & 0.45 & 0.6 \\ 0.15 & 0.25 & 0.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{65} \\ \frac{30}{65} \\ \frac{17}{65}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{65}+\frac{9}{65}+0 \\ \frac{6.3}{65}+\frac{13.5}{65}+\frac{10.2}{65} \\ \frac{2.7}{65}+\frac{7.5}{65}+\frac{6.8}{65}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{65} \\ \frac{30}{65} \\ \frac{17}{65}\end{aligned}]=q.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector such that $Pq=q.$ So, it's a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.75{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 75{x}_{1}-60{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9} \\ \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{9}=-\frac{1}{9}.$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 \\ 0.75 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-0.75{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 75{x}_{1}-60{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 5{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9} \\ \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{4}{9}-\frac{5}{9}=-\frac{1}{9}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
A factory produces two types of sugar: brown and extra-refined. Every year, the factory's sales executives study how customers' preferences change between the two types of sugar. The table below shows the results of this study.
From:
Brown Extra-Refined
To: Brown $0.8$ $1$
Extra-Refined $0.2$ $0$
It's found that $20%$ of customers who currently buy brown sugar will switch to extra-refined sugar next year, while $100%$ of customers who currently purchase extra-refined sugar will switch to brown sugar next year. Assuming that there are $450\,000$ customers in total and that the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many customers will eventually consume extra-refined sugar?
question.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, note that

$$
{P}^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.84 & 0.8 \\ 0.16 & 0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 1 \\ 0.2 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 \\ 0.2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=5{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 6{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{6} \\ \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{1}{6}$ of the customers will eventually use extra-refined sugar. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this type of sugar is

$$
