Question 3
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L2 follows from line L1 by
differentiating
integrating
adding Φ to
differentiating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
both sides of the equation.

Line L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the
initial system of ODEs
line L4
initial system of ODEs
solution of the system of ODEs
first shifting theorem
.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
adding Φ
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
integrating
adding Φ to
both sides of the equation.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next we consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t).

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}{e}^{t}-0\cdot {e}^{t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t} \\ 4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t} \\ 4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -2{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 4{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{-2}{3}{e}^{3t} \\ -4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{-2}{3}{e}^{3t} \\ -4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]. \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{10}{3} \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}(-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(1-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4(3t-1)+9(1-t) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3t+5 \\ 23-15t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

Question 3
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L2 follows from line L1 by
differentiating
integrating
adding Φ to
differentiating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
both sides of the equation.

Line L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the
initial system of ODEs
line L4
initial system of ODEs
solution of the system of ODEs
first shifting theorem
.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
adding Φ
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
integrating
adding Φ to
both sides of the equation.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next we consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t).

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next we consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t).

solution.reasoning: L2 differentiates L1 using the product rule. Substitution into the initial system of ODEs gives L3. Pre-multiplying L5 by the invertible fundamental matrix's inverse gives L6. Integrating L6 gives L7; integration constants may be set to zero when finding a particular solution. question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}},\,Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.
${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$ $-2{e}^{3t}$ $\,,\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$ $\frac{10}{3}$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}{e}^{t}-0\cdot {e}^{t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t} \\ 4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{3t} \\ 4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -2{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 4{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{-2}{3}{e}^{3t} \\ -4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{-2}{3}{e}^{3t} \\ -4{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]. \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{10}{3} \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+\,\,\frac{1}{9}$ {{field-1}} .
$23-15t$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}(-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(1-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4(3t-1)+9(1-t) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3t+5 \\ 23-15t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}(-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(1-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4(3t-1)+9(1-t) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3t+5 \\ 23-15t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The $1$rst row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The $1$st row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot {C}_{11}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+1\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-4)\cdot {C}_{22}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =(-4)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(2+3)+2(1+6) \\  & =-20+14 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $3$rd row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the third row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(3\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=-2\cdot 16=-32.
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{4+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(9-2) \\  & =-14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=-4\cdot (-14)=56.
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+5\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|+5|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-4)+5(6-3) \\  & =-3+15 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+2\cdot {C}_{22}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(5+4)+(0-2) \\  & =18-2 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 12-2\cdot 16=-20.
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.worked_solution:
The $2$nd row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have   

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23}+1\cdot {C}_{24} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{2+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$  determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+2\cdot {C}_{12}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(6-2)-(-6-2) \\  & =-8-(-8) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+2\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+(2)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-6-2)+2(0-6) \\  & =-(-8)+2\cdot (-6) \\  & =8-12 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=-0+(-4)=-4.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $2$nd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 7 & 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{12}+7\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{42} \\  & =7\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -3 & 9 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot {C}_{14}+0\cdot {C}_{24}+0\cdot {C}_{34}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =9\cdot (-1)^{1+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 7 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{13}+4\cdot {C}_{23}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{43} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
canonical_examples.problem:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th row, write the following determinant as a combination of $3 \times 3$ determinants:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251298/assets/aa7e4b76a38e068e3436b48783280bb8cb576a090494fe87e5afaeabf4e01722.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10 & 2 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 7 & 9 \\ -2 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -6 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & =(-6)\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+1\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-6)\cdot (-1)^{4+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 7 & 9 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{4+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}10 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 7 \\ -2 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =6\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 7 & 9 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}10 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 7 \\ -2 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251298/assets/8e2c555011024d6299a0c1330ab1f16c0aa346637668a897e284acfc94bd1c21.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{4+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-8)+(0-0) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column
canonical_examples.problem:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $2$nd column, write the following determinant as a combination of $3 \times 3$ determinants:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251298/assets/8f9383e07590f0b0e567ef8f1a7f754987aee083f6a7e843489c435f38bbf040.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 8 & 9 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{42} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 8 & 9 \\ 2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 8 & 9 \\ 2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes there are lots of calculations involved in finding the determinant of a matrix using a cofactor expansion across the first row. 

Fortunately, however, we don't always have to use the first row! We can use *any* row we like. A cofactor expansion across any general row is known as a **Laplace expansion**.

Across the row $i,$ the Laplace expansion of an $n\!\times\! n$ matrix $A$ is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}{C}_{ij} \\  & ={a}_{i1}{C}_{i1}+{a}_{i2}{C}_{i2}+⋯+{a}_{in}{C}_{in},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\color{blue}C_{ij}}$ is the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ in $A.$ Remember the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ is 

$$
{\color{black}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{black}M_{ij}},
$$

where ${\color{black}M_{ij}}$ is the minor of the entry.

For example, consider the following matrix:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251298/assets/b90691da28f0976a39a27ae68dea7b0c93ac1107f928d9aed402b106ffcba3b2.svg)

To compute the determinant of the matrix above, it is most convenient to use a Laplace expansion along the row with the most zeros. So, let's use Laplace expansion across the third row ($i=3$) as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{3j}{C}_{3j} \\  & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we reduced a $4 \times 4$ determinant to a $3 \times 3$ determinant.

tutorials.content:
Sometimes there are lots of calculations involved in finding the determinant of a matrix using a cofactor expansion across the first row. 

Fortunately, however, we don't always have to use the first row! We can use *any* row we like. A cofactor expansion across any general row is known as a **Laplace expansion**.

Across the row $i,$ the Laplace expansion of an $n\!\times\! n$ matrix $A$ is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}{C}_{ij} \\  & ={a}_{i1}{C}_{i1}+{a}_{i2}{C}_{i2}+⋯+{a}_{in}{C}_{in},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\color{blue}C_{ij}}$ is the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ in $A.$ Remember the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ is 

$$
{\color{black}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{black}M_{ij}},
$$

where ${\color{black}M_{ij}}$ is the minor of the entry.

For example, consider the following matrix:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251298/assets/b90691da28f0976a39a27ae68dea7b0c93ac1107f928d9aed402b106ffcba3b2.svg)

To compute the determinant of the matrix above, it is most convenient to use a Laplace expansion along the row with the most zeros. So, let's use Laplace expansion across the third row ($i=3$) as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{3j}{C}_{3j} \\  & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we reduced a $4 \times 4$ determinant to a $3 \times 3$ determinant.

tutorials.name: Laplace Expansion Across a Column
tutorials.problem:
We can also use the Laplace expansion across any *column* to find the determinant. Across the column $j,$ the Laplace expansion is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}{C}_{ij} \\  & ={a}_{1j}{C}_{1j}+{a}_{2j}{C}_{2j}+⋯+{a}_{nj}{C}_{nj},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\color{blue}C_{ij}$ is the cofactor of the entry ${\color{red}a_{ij}}.$

In other words, the Laplace expansion across a row or column is the sum of the entries in the row or column multiplied by their respective cofactors.

To find the determinant of a matrix, we can choose to use the Laplace expansion across any row or column, so choose the row or column that has the most zeros, to cut down on the calculations!

tutorial.content:
Sometimes there are lots of calculations involved in finding the determinant of a matrix using a cofactor expansion across the first row. 

Fortunately, however, we don't always have to use the first row! We can use *any* row we like. A cofactor expansion across any general row is known as a **Laplace expansion**.

Across the row $i,$ the Laplace expansion of an $n\!\times\! n$ matrix $A$ is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}{C}_{ij} \\  & ={a}_{i1}{C}_{i1}+{a}_{i2}{C}_{i2}+⋯+{a}_{in}{C}_{in},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\color{blue}C_{ij}}$ is the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ in $A.$ Remember the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ is 

$$
{\color{black}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{black}M_{ij}},
$$

where ${\color{black}M_{ij}}$ is the minor of the entry.

For example, consider the following matrix:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14251298/assets/5c9aa536eae832c2673a6855ecf768d79dcf064ee273405157fad1e57a6e428b.svg)

To compute the determinant of the matrix above, it is most convenient to use a Laplace expansion along the row with the most zeros. So, let's use Laplace expansion across the third row ($i=3$) as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{3j}{C}_{3j} \\  & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\end{aligned}
$$

So, we reduced a $4 \times 4$ determinant to a $3 \times 3$ determinant.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot {C}_{11}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{4+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-8)+(0-0) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$

$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

$$

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.

\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+5\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|+5|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-4)+5(6-3) \\  & =-3+15 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+2\cdot {C}_{22}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(5+4)+(0-2) \\  & =18-2 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 12-2\cdot 16=-20.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The $2$nd row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have   

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23}+1\cdot {C}_{24} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{2+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$  determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+2\cdot {C}_{12}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(6-2)-(-6-2) \\  & =-8-(-8) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+2\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+(2)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-6-2)+2(0-6) \\  & =-(-8)+2\cdot (-6) \\  & =8-12 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=-0+(-4)=-4.
$$

tutorial.name: Laplace Expansion Across a Column
tutorial.problem:
We can also use the Laplace expansion across any *column* to find the determinant. Across the column $j,$ the Laplace expansion is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}{C}_{ij} \\  & ={a}_{1j}{C}_{1j}+{a}_{2j}{C}_{2j}+⋯+{a}_{nj}{C}_{nj},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\color{blue}C_{ij}$ is the cofactor of the entry ${\color{red}a_{ij}}.$

In other words, the Laplace expansion across a row or column is the sum of the entries in the row or column multiplied by their respective cofactors.

To find the determinant of a matrix, we can choose to use the Laplace expansion across any row or column, so choose the row or column that has the most zeros, to cut down on the calculations!

observed_steps.name: Question 11
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ -7 & 2 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+-7\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{41} \\  & =(-7)\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ -7 & 2 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+-7\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{41} \\  & =(-7)\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -3 & 9 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot {C}_{14}+0\cdot {C}_{24}+0\cdot {C}_{34}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =9\cdot (-1)^{1+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 7 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{13}+4\cdot {C}_{23}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{43} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the Laplace expansion across a row or column is the sum of the entries in the row or column multiplied by their respective cofactors.

To find the determinant of a matrix, we can choose to use the Laplace expansion across any row or column, so choose the row or column that has the most zeros, to cut down on the calculations!

question.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
last_observation.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

solution.reasoning: Expanding along row 3, the nonzero entries are a32 = -5 and a33 = -5. Their cofactor signs are (-1)^(3+2) = -1 and (-1)^(3+3) = +1, giving 5 det(M32) - 5 det(M33), exactly option d. The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
last_observation.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
last_observation.worked_solution:
The $1$rst row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

?

|2030412−310−2−1−1152|=

a
−2⋅|12−30−2−1−152|−3⋅|41−310−1−112|
b
−2⋅|12−30−2−1152|+3⋅|41−310−1−112|
c
2⋅|12−30−2−1152|+3⋅|41−310−1−112|
d
2⋅|12−30−2−1−152|−3⋅|41−310−1−112|
e
4⋅|12−30−2−1152|+3⋅|41−310−1−112|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The 1rst row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the 1st row, we have

|2030412−310−2−1−1152|=2⋅C11+0⋅C12+3⋅C13+0⋅C14=2⋅(−1)1+1|12−30−2−1152|+3⋅(−1)1+3⋅|41−310−1−112|=2⋅|12−30−2−1152|+3⋅|41−310−1−112|.
question.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

solution.reasoning: Expanding along row 1 gives two nonzero terms, at columns 1 and 3. Both cofactor signs are positive, so the expansion is 2 det(M11) + 3 det(M13). Deleting column 1 leaves the final minor row (1,5,2), exactly as in option c. No answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.worked_solution:
The $1$rst row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
last_observation.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The 3rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the 3rd row, we have

|1−21242−3100025−1−22|=0⋅C31+0⋅C32+0⋅C33+2⋅C34=2⋅(−1)3+4⋅|1−2142−35−1−2|=−2⋅|1−2142−35−1−2|.
question.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

solution.reasoning: Expanding along row 3 leaves only the entry 2 in column 4. Its cofactor sign is (-1)^{3+4}=-1, giving -2 times the determinant obtained by deleting row 3 and column 4, exactly option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is provided; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot {C}_{11}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
last_observation.worked_solution:
The $1$st row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot {C}_{11}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

|5−2002−3−2572433−62−8|=

a
5⋅|−3−25243−62−8|−2⋅|2−2574332−8|
b
2⋅|−3−25243−62−8|−5⋅|2−2574332−8|
c
2⋅|2−2574332−8|

5⋅|−3−25243−62−8|+4⋅|2−2574332−8|
e
5⋅|−3−25243−62−8|+2⋅|2−2574332−8|

Correct
EXPLANATION

The 1st row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the 1st row, we have

|5−2002−3−2572433−62−8|=5⋅C11+(−2)⋅C12+0⋅C13+0⋅C14=5⋅(−1)1+1|−3−25243−62−8|+(−2)⋅(−1)1+2⋅|2−2574332−8|=5⋅|−3−25243−62−8|+2⋅|2−2574332−8|.
question.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

solution.reasoning: Expanding along row 1 gives 5 det(M11) + (-2)(-1) det(M12) = 5 det(M11) + 2 det(M12), exactly option e. The remaining entries in that row are zero. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot {C}_{11}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+1\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-4)\cdot {C}_{22}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =(-4)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(2+3)+2(1+6) \\  & =-20+14 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.
$$

$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{4+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(9-2) \\  & =-14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=-4\cdot (-14)=56.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The $2$nd row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have   

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23}+1\cdot {C}_{24} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{2+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$  determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+2\cdot {C}_{12}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(6-2)-(-6-2) \\  & =-8-(-8) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+2\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+(2)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-6-2)+2(0-6) \\  & =-(-8)+2\cdot (-6) \\  & =8-12 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=-0+(-4)=-4.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column
last_observation.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ -7 & 2 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+-7\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{41} \\  & =(-7)\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

?

a
7⋅|−11573−22−4−1|

|31572−32−3−1|

−7⋅|31572−32−3−1|

3|315−3272−3−1|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using a cofactor expansion along the 1st column, we have

|0315−72−41072−302−3−1|=0⋅C11+−7⋅C21+0⋅C31+0⋅C41=(−7)⋅(−1)2+1⋅|31572−32−3−1|=7⋅|31572−32−3−1|.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column

solution.reasoning: Expanding along column 1 leaves only the entry -7 in row 2. Its cofactor sign is (-1)^{2+1}=-1, so the coefficient is +7. Deleting row 2 and column 1 yields exactly the minor in option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 1 & 5 \\ -7 & 2 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+-7\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{41} \\  & =(-7)\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column
last_observation.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $2$nd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 7 & 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{12}+7\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{42} \\  & =7\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

|20−13172−1−3012−203−1|=

a
3⋅|2−13321−23−1|
b
−7⋅|2−13−312−23−1|
c
5⋅|2−1321−3−13−2|
d
7⋅|2−13−312−23−1|
e
7⋅|2−1312−1−23−1|
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Using a cofactor expansion along the 2nd column, we have

|20−13172−1−3012−203−1|=0⋅C12+7⋅C22+0⋅C32+0⋅C42=7⋅(−1)2+2⋅|2−13−312−23−1|=7⋅|2−13−312−23−1|.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column

solution.reasoning: Expanding along column 2 leaves only the entry 7 in row 2. Its cofactor sign is (-1)^{2+2}=1. Deleting row 2 and column 2 gives exactly the minor in option d, with coefficient 7. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different matrix.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $2$nd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 7 & 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{12}+7\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{42} \\  & =7\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =7\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column
last_observation.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -3 & 9 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot {C}_{14}+0\cdot {C}_{24}+0\cdot {C}_{34}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =9\cdot (-1)^{1+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$
